Claims 6 and 7 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 as allegedly being directed to an abstract idea without significantly more.
Applicant respectfully traverses these rejections for at least the following reasons.

M.P.E.P. § 2106 sets forth two criteria for subject matter eligibility for a claimed invention. First, the claimed invention must be to one of the four statutory categories set forth in 35 U.S.C. § 101: processes, machines, manufactures and compositions of matter. Second, "the claimed invention also must qualify as patent-eligible subject matter, i.e., the claim must not be directed to a judicial exception unless the claim as a whole includes additional limitations amounting to significantly more than the exception." MPEP § 2106.

Applicant respectfully submits that the pending claims each fall within a statutory category of 35 U.S.C. § 101. For example, Claim 6 is directed to a method and Claim 7 is directed to an item of manufacture. The Office Action appears to assert that the claims fall within one of the four statutory categories. See Office Action, p. 3. Thus, the parties appear to agree that the claims qualify for patentability as one of statutory classes of inventions. (Step 1: YES)

p.u: Claims Are Not Directed to a Judicial Exception

body.p: M.P.E.P. § 2106.04 sets forth the analysis Examiners are to apply when determining whether a claimed invention is directed to a judicial exception, such as an abstract idea. The
purpose of step 2A is to determine whether the claim as a whole is directed to a judicial exception. See MPEP § 2106.04. M.P.E.P. § 2106.04 cautions that "[e]xaminers should . . . . be careful to

distinguish claims that recite an exception (which require further eligibility analysis) and claims that merely involve an exception (which are eligible and do not require further eligibility analysis)." Id. at § 2106.04(II)(A)(1) (emphasis in original).

The Office Action alleges that Claims 6 and 7 cover "mental processes", Applicant respectfully disagrees. See Office Action, pp. 4-6. MPEP § 2106(III)(A) instructs that "[c]laims do not recite a mental process when they do not contain limitations that can practically be performed in the human mind, for instance when the human mind is not equipped to perform the claim limitations." MPEP § 2106(III)(A) (citing SRIInt'l, Inc. v. Cisco Systems, Inc., 930 F.3d 1295, 1304 (Fed. Cir. 2019) (declining to identify the claimed collection and analysis of network data as abstract because "the human mind is not equipped to detect suspicious activity by using network monitors and analyzing network packets as recited by the claims"); CyberSource, 654 F.3d at 1376, 99 USPQ2d at 1699 (distinguishing Research Corp. Techs. v. Microsoft Corp., 627 F.3d 859, 97 USPQ2d 1274 (Fed. Cir. 2010), and SiRF Tech., Inc. v. Int'l Trade Comm'n, 601 F.3d 1319, 94 USPQ2d 1607 (Fed. Cir. 2010), as directed to inventions that "could not, as a practical matter, be performed entirely in a human's mind").

As the human mind is not equipped to perform automated driving control of a vehicle by automatically performing a driving operation of the vehicle relating to a driving plan of the vehicle, provide a driver with a driving event that is to occur at a point ahead in a direction of advance from a current point, judge whether a driver driving operation being performed by the driver at a point before the point of the driving event is acceptable to be performed, and provide the driver with judgment information indicating that the driver not perform the driver driving operation, such

Applicant respectfully submits that, under the guidance discussed above, the claims are not directed to a judicial exception such as an abstract idea. The claims do not recite a basic concept that is similar to any abstract idea previously identified by the courts. For example, Claims 6 and 7 do not recite any mathematical concept or a mental process that can be performed in the human mind or by a human using a pen and paper. Instead, Claims 6 and 7 are necessarily rooted in technology requiring performing automated driving control of a vehicle by automatically performing a driving operation of the vehicle relating to a driving plan of the vehicle, providing a driver with a driving event that is to occur at a point ahead in a direction of advance from a current point, judging whether a driver driving operation being performed by the driver at a point before the point of the driving event is acceptable to be performed, and providing the driver with judgment information indicating that the driver not perform the driver driving operation. For at least these reasons, Applicant's claims are not directed to a judicial exception. (Step 2A Pron One: NO)

Even assuming for the sake of argument only that Claim 1 is found to include a judicial exception under Prong One of Step 2A, the claims are not "directed to" a judicial exception under Prong Two of Step 2A. In particular, under Step 2A Prong Two, the claims are analyzed to

determine whether the claims as a whole integrate the recited judicial exception into a practical application of that exception. See MPEP § 2106.04(d). Additional limitations recited in the claim amount to significantly more than the abstract idea if the additional limitations improve the functioning of a computer or another technology. See id.

While Applicant disagrees with these allegations, to advance prosecution, Applicant has amended independent Claims 6 and 7 to clarify the practical application integration of step 2A, prong 2 of the 2019 PEG. For example, Claim 6 recites an information provision method for controlling a vehicle that includes:
" performing automated driving control of the vehicle by automatically performing a
driving operation of the vehicle relating to a driving plan of the vehicle, the automated driving control comprising operations relating to at least one of acceleration, steering,
and braking, according to the driving plan;
" providing a driver, through an information provision device mounted in the vehicle,
with a driving event that is to occur at a point ahead in a direction of advance from a current point, based on the driving plan of the vehicle prepared during the automated
driving control;
" judging whether a driver driving operation being performed by the driver at a point
before the point of the driving event is acceptable to be performed, the driving event being a lane change, and the driver driving operation being a lane change at the point
before the point of the driving event; and
" providing the driver with judgment information indicating that the driver not perform

the driver driving operation, based on the judging that the driver driving operation is unacceptable according to the driving plan being performed, the judgment information comprising lane change inhibiting information indicating that a lane to be changed to is unable to be driven on between the point before the point of the driving event and the point of the driving event due to at least one of a lane blockage or ending of the
lane to be changed to.

These operations provide a way for "a driver can judge based on the judgment information whether it is suitable to perform in advance a driving operation corresponding to a scheduled driving event to be performed in the future." See, e.g., Specification, [0011]. In addition, the operations recited in Claim 6 include meaningful limitations that add more than generally linking

the use of an abstract idea to a particular technological environment because they solve a real problem with a solution that improves the functioning of an information provision device and provides an improved user interface for the information provision device to increase the efficiency of using the information provision device, similar to Core Wireless. See MPEP § 2106.05(a)(I)(x) (citing Core Wireless Licensing S.A.R.L., v. LG Electronics, Inc., 880 F.3d 1356, 1362-63, 125 USPQ2d 1436, 1440-41 (Fed. Cir. 2018)). These limitations provide unconventional steps that integrate Claim 6 to a practical application, and improve the way autonomous driving vehicles perform.

Therefore, Applicant respectfully asserts that Claim 6 recites patent eligible subject matter. To the extent that independent Claim 7 recites features similar to the above-noted features of Claim 6, Applicant submits that Claim 7 recites patent eligible subject matter for at least reasons similar to those discussed above with respect to Claim 6. (Step 2A Pronm Two: YES)

Under Step 2B, the claims are analyzed to determine whether there are additional limitations recited in the claims that amount to significantly more than the abstract idea, either individually or as an ordered combination. See MPEP § 2106.05. However, it is not necessary to reach this analysis in this case because Applicant's claims are directed to a statutory category (Step 1) and are not directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A). (Step 2B: N/A)
For at least these reasons, Applicant respectfully submits that Claim 6 and 7 is directed to patent eligible subject matter, and respectfully requests reconsideration and allowance of the claims.
Claims 1 and 3-7 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as purportedly being unpatentable
over Ratnasingam (US 9,672,734), in view of Abe (US 2019/0113914), and in further view of
Watanabe (US 2018/0105185).
Applicant respectfully traverses these rejections for at least the following reasons and
discusses independent Claim 1 as an example.
Without any admissions, independent Claim 1 has been amended to recite:
A vehicle control device configured to control a vehicle, comprising:
an information provision device configured to provide information to a
driver of the vehicle;

a processor, during automated driving control of the vehicle, configured to: perform the automated driving control by automatically performing a driving operation of the vehicle relating to a driving plan of the vehicle control device, the automated driving control comprising operations relating to at least one of acceleration, steering, and braking, according to
the driving plan;
provide, through the information provision device to the driver, a driving event that is to occur at a point ahead in a direction of advance from
a current point, based on an automated driving plan;

judge whether a driver driving operation being performed by the driver at a point before the point of the driving event is acceptable to be performed, the driving event being a lane change, and the driver driving operation being a lane change at the point before the point of the driving
event; and

provide the driver with judgment information indicating that the driver not perform the driver driving operation, based on the judging that the driver driving operation is unacceptable according to the driving plan being executed by the vehicle control device, the judgment information comprising lane change inhibiting information indicating that a lane to be changed to is unable to be driven on between the point before the point of the driving event and the point of the driving event due to at
least one of a lane blockage or ending of the lane to be changed to.

At a minimum, the proposed Ratnasingam-Abe-Watanabe combination does not disclose, teach, or suggest that "the judgment information comprising lane change inhibiting information indicating that a lane to be changed to is unable to be driven on between the point before the point of the driving event and the point of the driving event due to at least one of a lane blockage or ending of the lane to be changed to," as recited in Claim 1.

The Office Action acknowledges that Ratnasingam and Abe do not teach the cited features of Claim 1. See Office Action, pp. 14-15 (citing Claim 1 prior to the present amendments). Instead, the Office Action relies on Watanabe as allegedly disclosing these features. Applicant respectfully submits that Watanabe does not make up for at least the above-discussed deficiencies of Ratnasingam and Abe.

Watanabe discloses, referring to FIG. 71, an image generator that "generates an image in which the inexecutable action ('lane change to right' 1202) is displayed in a display manner, different from the display manner of the other executable actions, where the icon indicating the inexecutable action is grayed out or the luminance of the icon is reduced":
FIG 71

According to Watanabe, "the action basis that 'lane change to right' should not be executed is approaching adjacent following vehicle 1103 in the right lane." Id. at [0599]. For example, Watanabe discloses that enclosing "the icon representing adjacent following vehicle 1103 by shaded image 1353 indicates that the approaching of adjacent following vehicle 1103 is a negative basis that lane 'change to right' should not be executed." Id.

Watanabe further discloses, referring to FIG. 58C, an action candidate determination unit "sums the values (number of selected times) of the selected columns for each action (for each row)", "determines, as a recommended action, the action in which the total of the number of selected times is the maximum", and "selects, as an inexecutable action, the action in which the values (number of selected times) of the selected columns include zero." Id. at [0555]-[0556].

That is, at best, Watanabe discloses indicating to the driver that an action should not be performed based either on the driver's past driving history (e.g., a driver model constructed by the action candidate determination unit) or an approaching adjacent following vehicle (e.g., vehicle 1103 of FIG. 71).

To the extent the Office is attempting to equate the icon indicating the inexecutable action of Watanabe to the claimed "lane change inhibiting information", Claim 1 recites that "the judgment information comprising lane change inhibiting information indicating that a lane to be changed to is unable to be driven on between the point before the point of the driving event and the point of the driving event due to at least one of a lane blockage or ending of the lane to be changed to." Watanabe does not disclose that is inexecutable action is based on a lane that is unable to be driven on between the point before the point of the driving event and the point of the driving event, much less that the lane is unable to be driven due to at least one of a lane blockage or ending of the lane to be changed to. Therefore, Watanabe's purported disclosure of an icon indicating an inexecutable action does not disclose the claimed "lane change inhibiting information".
Consequently, Watanabe does not disclose, teach, or suggest at least the cited features recited in Claim 1.

Thus, even assuming for the sake of argument only that the proposed Ratnasingam-Abe- Watanabe combination would have been proper, which Applicant does not concede, the proposed combination does not disclose, teach, or suggest all features recited in Claim 1.
In view of the above, Applicant respectfully submits that Claim 1 is patentable over the cited references and requests withdrawal of the rejection.

To the extent that independent Claims 6 and 7 recite features similar to the above-noted features of Claim 1, Applicant submits that Claims 6 and 7 are patentable for at least reasons similar to those discussed above with respect to Claim 1.
Applicant respectfully submits that dependent Claims 3 and 4 are patentable due to their respective dependencies, as well as for their additional features. This should not be construed as

an acquiescence to Examiner's interpretation of the claims, or reading of those claim elements on the prior art, and Applicant expressly reserves the right to establish the patentability of those additional claim limitations, should the need arise. Conclusion
